title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an example of AI-generated impersonation deployed as part of an investment fraud scheme. Scammers used deepfake technology to fabricate a fake interview featuring real, recognisable public figures, placing those likenesses inside a false news article designed to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The failure is not in a company's AI product malfunctioning, but in AI tools being deliberately applied by bad actors outside any sanctioned deployment, to manufacture false evidence of real events that never occurred.

The deception was layered: fake articles, fake websites, and fake reviews were constructed together before victims were contacted directly by phone. This layering means no single point of detection would have been sufficient, and ordinary cues that consumers use to assess legitimacy, polished presentation and familiar faces, were precisely what the scheme exploited. The scale ASIC reported, tens of thousands of takedowns in a single year, indicates this is not isolated experimentation but an operational pattern.

What is not established is who specifically produced the deepfake content, whether any criminal charges have followed, or that any particular AI platform or tool vendor bears responsibility for these uses.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claimed that Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had an angry confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler over an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never actually occurred. This type of scam, which uses artificial intelligence to create deepfake content featuring well-known Australians, is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, along with politicians like Pauline Hanson and business figures including Alan Kohler and Dick Smith, are frequently impersonated in these schemes.

ASIC's enforcement efforts removed 19,400 scams last year, representing a 182 percent increase from the previous year. The regulator took down 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. These schemes typically build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and reviews to establish credibility before targeting victims with scripted phone calls and requests for investment. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding alone do not indicate legitimacy.
